paragraphs: Semi-structured neural networks combine structured regression with a deep neural network. The attraction is that different parts of the model can offer interpretability, flexible predictions, and statistically grounded uncertainty estimates. But interpreting their contributions requires identifiability: a way to distinguish what each component contributes rather than allowing overlapping explanations.

The paper shows that techniques used to enforce this separation can interfere with learning. They can produce worse estimates, slow convergence, and lead to degraded or incorrect predictions. The proposed solution is post-hoc orthogonalization, or PHO, which addresses component separation after fitting through a non-invasive adjustment.

The authors establish that PHO guarantees identifiable model components while preserving favorable properties of semi-structured models, and report better estimation and prediction quality. Numerical experiments, a benchmark comparison, and an application to COVID-19 infections support their theoretical findings. The contribution is a way to reconcile meaningful component interpretation with effective fitting, addressing a conflict introduced by existing identification techniques.
icml-2023-a-new-pho-rmula-for-improved-p.tldr: Post-hoc orthogonalization makes semi-structured network components identifiable while improving estimation and prediction quality.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to rank experts when their performance can be measured across many tasks, but each measurement is noisy. Its central assumption is strong: for any pair of experts, the better expert performs better on every task. Thus, tasks provide different opportunities to gather evidence about a consistent underlying ordering.

The learner operates sequentially, choosing which expert to evaluate on which task using information collected so far. The authors give strategies for recovering the correct ranking and bound the number of evaluations with probability at least one minus a chosen failure tolerance. These bounds depend on the particular problem instance, allowing the analysis to reflect differences in difficulty.

Matching lower bounds, up to polylogarithmic factors, show that the proposed evaluation requirements are close to the theoretical limits in this setting. The authors also adapt the strategy to identifying only the best expert. Numerical simulations agree with the theory, supporting adaptive evaluation as a way to avoid unnecessary measurements under the shared-ordering assumption.
icml-2023-active-ranking-of-experts-base.tldr: Adaptive evaluations can efficiently rank experts under an assumption that their relative performance order is consistent across tasks.

paragraphs: A monotonic prediction must move in a specified direction when a relevant input increases. Such constraints are useful when a model must respect known relationships, particularly in areas such as finance and healthcare. A traditional neural-network construction enforces monotonicity by restricting weight signs, but with popular unsaturated activations this approach can only approximate convex functions.

The paper expands that construction by deriving two additional activation functions from a typical unsaturated monotonic activation. Different subsets of neurons use these related activations. This preserves the desired monotonic behavior while overcoming the restriction to convex shapes, making the model capable of expressing a broader range of constrained relationships.

The authors prove that the resulting network can approximate any continuous monotone function on a compact subset of a finite-dimensional real space. Their experiments report better accuracy than the compared state-of-the-art methods with fewer parameters. The construction also requires neither changes to the learning procedure nor additional steps after learning, making the expressiveness result relevant to a comparatively simple training workflow.
icml-2023-constrained-monotonic-neural-n.tldr: A simple activation-function construction makes sign-constrained monotonic networks more expressive without changing their training procedure.

paragraphs: Multilingual language models aim to share useful information across languages, potentially including languages not encountered during training. Alongside this goal, developers may want privacy, linguistic fairness, and transparency about how training examples affect predictions. The paper asks whether these objectives can be achieved together, rather than treating each as a separate design problem.

Its theoretical results distinguish two situations. Multilingual compression and linguistic fairness are compatible with differential privacy. However, differential privacy conflicts with sparse training-data influence, a transparency objective in which influence is concentrated among relatively few training examples. The conflict concerns this particular form of transparency rather than establishing that all transparency is incompatible with privacy.

The authors also conduct experiments on two common language-processing tasks, examining multilingual compression and influence sparsity under different privacy guarantees. These experiments explore how the theoretical tensions appear in practice. The findings motivate jointly optimizing the objectives to identify workable trade-offs, instead of assuming that improving privacy, fairness, compression, and sparse attribution independently will produce a satisfactory combined model.
icml-2023-differential-privacy-linguisti.tldr: Differential privacy is compatible with multilingual compression and linguistic fairness but conflicts with sparse training-data influence.

paragraphs: The paper considers multiple agents learning a linear bandit problem together. They aim to reduce their combined cumulative regret, meaning the accumulated performance loss from their decisions. Collaboration occurs through a central server, but communication in both directions uses fixed-capacity channels, so each channel use can carry only a limited amount of information.

The authors first establish information-theoretic lower bounds on the number of communicated bits required to obtain sublinear regret. This makes communication an explicit resource in the analysis, rather than assuming that agents can freely exchange everything they learn. The lower bounds provide a target against which a distributed algorithm can be assessed.

They then develop an efficient algorithm that matches the minimum sublinear regret order available through centralized learning while using the minimum communication order specified by those bounds. These are order-level guarantees rather than claims of exact equality in every cost. For sparse linear bandits, a variant exploits the problem's sparsity to improve the balance between communication and regret further.
icml-2023-distributed-linear-bandits-und.tldr: A distributed linear-bandit algorithm matches centralized regret scaling with communication scaling that meets information-theoretic lower bounds.

paragraphs: Clustering groups data without supplied labels, but deciding which group each item belongs to creates a discrete optimization problem. That discrete assignment is awkward to integrate into a fully differentiable learning system. The paper connects clustering assignments to associative memories, neural networks whose recursive dynamics support the recovery or completion of patterns.

Using this connection, the authors propose ClAM, an unconstrained continuous relaxation of the clustering problem. Replacing the discrete formulation with this relaxation allows clustering to participate in end-to-end gradient-based learning. They also develop a self-supervised clustering loss that draws on associative memories' pattern-completion ability, providing a training signal without externally supplied cluster labels.

Evaluations across varied datasets show that the self-supervised component helps ClAM. The authors report improvements over both Lloyd's k-means algorithm and more recent continuous relaxations, reaching up to 60% on the Silhouette Coefficient. This is a reported maximum improvement on that clustering-quality measure, while the broader contribution is the link between memory dynamics, continuous clustering, and self-supervised training.
icml-2023-end-to-end-differentiable-clus.tldr: ClAM uses associative-memory dynamics and a self-supervised loss to make clustering differentiable and improve measured clustering quality.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization concerns decisions whose outcomes depend on uncertain quantities. In end-to-end learning, a trained decision map directly produces an action or solution. This paper examines what the standard training approach is actually learning, giving it a Bayesian interpretation rather than treating it solely as a convenient computational procedure.

The authors show that the standard algorithm trains a posterior Bayes action map: a mapping associated with choosing actions under posterior uncertainty. They use that interpretation to design additional algorithms for learning decision maps that output solutions to empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization problems. These correspond to two distinct ways of formulating decisions under uncertainty.

Experiments on a synthetic newsvendor problem illustrate differences between the training schemes. A real-data economic dispatch problem also examines how the neural-network architecture of a decision map affects test performance. Together, the analysis and examples clarify that both the optimization principle represented by training and the architecture used to express decisions can matter when evaluating an end-to-end decision system.
icml-2023-end-to-end-learning-for-stocha.tldr: A Bayesian interpretation of end-to-end decision learning leads to new training methods for empirical-risk and distributionally robust optimization.

paragraphs: The top-k operator keeps the largest input values and sets the others to zero. This produces sparse selections, but abrupt changes in which values are selected make the operator difficult to train through with backpropagation. The paper seeks operators that combine differentiability with sparsity, properties that earlier relaxations had not fully provided together.

The authors express top-k selection as a linear optimization problem over the permutahedron, a shape formed from permutations. Adding a p-norm regularization term smooths the operation. They show that computing the resulting operators reduces to isotonic optimization, which imposes ordering constraints, and their framework also accommodates selection according to magnitude.

For computation, the paper provides pool adjacent violator algorithms and introduces a Dykstra algorithm designed to suit GPUs and TPUs. The operators are successfully used for neural-network weight pruning, vision-transformer fine-tuning, and routing in sparse mixtures of experts. These applications illustrate how a trainable selection mechanism can retain sparsity while becoming usable inside larger end-to-end learning systems.
icml-2023-fast-differentiable-and-sparse.tldr: A convex-optimization framework produces differentiable sparse top-k operators with algorithms suited to modern accelerators.

paragraphs: Geometric Clifford Algebra Networks are designed to model dynamical systems using geometric transformations as building blocks. The paper develops this approach through geometric, or Clifford, algebra, with distance-preserving transformations encoded as elements of the Pin group. This supplies a mathematical language for representing transformations of geometric objects within a neural network.

The central architectural idea is a group action layer. Such a layer linearly combines transformations of objects using group actions specified in advance. Combined with new activation and normalization schemes, these layers act as adjustable geometric templates. Gradient descent refines the templates, allowing learning to operate within the proposed transformation-based representation.

The authors evaluate the approach on three-dimensional rigid-body transformations and large-scale fluid-dynamics simulations. They report significantly better performance than traditional methods and describe the results as strong empirical support for the architecture's theoretical advantages. The significance is that geometric transformations become part of the model's computational structure, with the reported applications showing benefits for two kinds of dynamical-system modeling.
icml-2023-geometric-clifford-algebra-net.tldr: GCANs learn geometric transformation templates and report improved modeling of rigid-body transformations and fluid dynamics.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends on informative comparisons among examples. One common strategy mines difficult negative examples, but this can lengthen training epochs and require maintaining nearest-neighbor indexes or repeatedly searching recent batches. The paper approaches the problem through batch composition, asking how existing samples should be grouped to make training comparisons more useful.

The proposed Global Contrastive Batch Sampling method, or GCBS, efficiently approximates a batch-assignment problem tied to an upper bound on the gap between global and training losses. Its focus on sample arrangement offers an alternative to adding mined negatives. It leaves the model itself unchanged and does not maintain external nearest-neighbor data structures.

Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art performance on sentence-embedding and code-search tasks. The authors also report that GCBS is more computationally efficient than even minimal hard-negative mining approaches and needs only a few additional lines of code. The results make batch selection a consequential part of contrastive learning, with benefits demonstrated through both task performance and computational efficiency.
icml-2023-global-selection-of-contrastiv.tldr: GCBS improves contrastive learning by optimizing batch assignments, reducing mining overhead while improving sentence-embedding and code-search results.

paragraphs: Hierarchical vision transformers have accumulated specialized components intended to improve supervised image classification. These additions can deliver good accuracy and appealing arithmetic-operation counts while still making execution slower than a simpler vision transformer. The paper investigates whether strong pretraining can remove the need for that architectural complexity.

Starting from a state-of-the-art multi-stage vision transformer, the authors use MAE, a strong visual pretraining task, and remove the specialized additions without losing accuracy. The resulting architecture, Hiera, retains a hierarchical structure while simplifying the network. The argument therefore connects architectural simplicity to the capabilities supplied through pretraining.

The authors report that Hiera is more accurate than previous models and significantly faster during both training and inference. They evaluate it across image- and video-recognition tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the simplified design in the tested settings and highlight why operation counts alone do not settle practical efficiency: the complexity of the operations and architecture also affects observed execution speed.
icml-2023-hiera-a-hierarchical-vision-tr.tldr: Hiera combines strong MAE pretraining with a simplified hierarchical transformer to improve accuracy and training and inference speed.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses noisy information to make progress toward a solution. A guarantee about average behavior does not directly specify what happens with high probability in a particular run. This paper develops finite-time, high-probability convergence guarantees while relaxing noise assumptions used by existing results, including assumptions of bounded variance.

The authors instead assume a bounded central moment of order alpha, where alpha is greater than one and at most two. When alpha is below two, this condition can accommodate noise without bounded variance. The analysis still imposes a quantitative restriction on the noise, but permits a broader class than analyses requiring a finite second moment.

Several algorithms receive guarantees across smooth minimization settings, including non-convex problems and multiple convexity-related conditions. The paper also covers variational inequalities under specified regularity and monotonicity conditions. Its contribution is theoretical justification for the considered methods in these broader settings, extending high-confidence convergence analysis to problems whose noise or structural properties fall outside commonly studied assumptions.
icml-2023-high-probability-bounds-for-st.tldr: New high-probability convergence guarantees allow stochastic optimization noise with bounded lower-order moments even when variance may be unbounded.

paragraphs: Some datasets contain entire probability distributions as individual observations. Comparing two collections then requires accounting for where those distributions live, which might be an interval, a circle, a sphere, another manifold, or a graph. This paper develops a statistical approach that can handle these varied domains within a common construction.

The authors introduce intrinsic slicing to define a new class of Wasserstein distances on manifolds and graphs. These distances admit embeddings into a Hilbert space. That property lets the comparison of distribution collections become a more familiar test of means in the embedding space, connecting a geometric comparison problem to established statistical machinery.

The paper provides two testing procedures: one uses resampling, and the other combines p-values from tests on individual coordinates. Experiments on synthetic and real data report strong detection power and well-calibrated p-values. These findings indicate that the proposed tests can detect differences while producing meaningful statistical significance assessments in the evaluated settings, across domains where a single conventional representation would be restrictive.
icml-2023-intrinsic-sliced-wasserstein-d.tldr: Intrinsic slicing turns comparisons of distribution collections on manifolds and graphs into mean tests in a Hilbert space.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems often aim to increase engagement, but continually encouraging consumption can contribute to burnout, departure, or addictive habits. Break reminders offer a possible intervention, yet manually configured reminders may serve neither users nor the platform well. This paper studies how a recommendation system could learn when to suggest breaks to sustain engagement over time.

The framework models recommendation dynamics using a Lotka-Volterra dynamical system. Its starting point is that engagement responds to both positive and negative feedback. Within this model, choosing breaks becomes an optimal-control problem: the system selects interventions based on how they affect the modeled evolution of engagement.

The authors provide an efficient learning algorithm and theoretical guarantees, then demonstrate its utility using semi-synthetic data. The stated empirical evidence therefore concerns that evaluation setting. The contribution is a formal way to incorporate breaks into long-term recommendation objectives, making interruption part of the decision process rather than treating continued consumption as the only desirable immediate action.
icml-2023-learning-to-suggest-breaks-sus.tldr: A dynamical-system framework learns break policies intended to sustain long-term engagement, with theoretical guarantees and semi-synthetic evaluation.

paragraphs: Graph clustering groups vertices according to relationships encoded by edges. Methods based on the graph p-Laplacian offer a parameter that changes which cluster structures are favored, but computing their third and higher eigenvectors is difficult. This paper explores effective p-resistance as an alternative route to clustering a graph into multiple groups.

The parameter p gives this resistance measure an interpretable structural preference. Small values favor clusters with strong internal connectivity, while large values favor clusters with smaller extent, expressed through shorter paths between vertices. Exact p-resistance is expensive to compute, so the authors develop an approximation to make this approach more accessible computationally.

They prove upper and lower bounds for the approximation and establish that it is exact on trees. They also provide theoretical justification for using p-resistance in clustering and compare the resulting method with other p-Laplacian approaches experimentally. The contribution combines a controllable notion of cluster structure with a bounded approximation, avoiding reliance on the difficult higher-eigenvector calculations that motivated the work.
icml-2023-multi-class-graph-clustering-v.tldr: An approximation to effective p-resistance supports graph clustering with tunable structural preferences and is exact for trees.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a decision policy would perform using data collected under another policy. When there are many possible actions, conventional importance weighting can produce excessive variance. This paper proposes OffCEM, an estimator that divides the action effect into a shared cluster effect and an action-specific residual effect.

OffCEM applies importance weighting at the level of action clusters and estimates residual reward effects with a model. The authors prove unbiasedness under a condition called local correctness. This condition requires the residual model to preserve relative expected-reward differences among actions within each cluster; it does not demand that every modeled reward level be exactly correct.

A two-step estimation procedure first minimizes bias and then variance, reflecting the two components of the approach. The authors report substantial bias and variance improvements over a range of conventional estimators, with experiments showing particular benefits when the action space is large. The result connects reduced weighting variance to a precise modeling requirement, making the role of within-cluster reward accuracy explicit.
icml-2023-off-policy-evaluation-for-larg.tldr: OffCEM combines cluster-level importance weighting with residual reward modeling to improve evaluation of policies with many actions.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization often uses a surrogate model to predict which configurations are worth evaluating next. Uncertainty estimates help guide that search. Gaussian processes are a common choice, but their assumptions about observation noise may not match practical evaluations. This paper proposes conformalized quantile regression as an alternative surrogate approach.

The method makes minimal assumptions about observation noise, allowing the target function to be modeled more robustly and realistically in the authors' formulation. Its purpose is to improve the information used to choose subsequent evaluations. On empirical benchmarks, the authors report faster hyperparameter-optimization convergence, linking the alternative uncertainty treatment to practical search efficiency.

The paper also extends the approach to multi-fidelity optimization, where evaluations can use different resource levels. A simple aggregation technique combines observations across those levels. The authors report that this technique outperforms conventional methods across many empirical tasks. Together, the contributions address both noisy evaluations and the problem of using results obtained with different computational commitments within one search.
icml-2023-optimizing-hyperparameters-wit.tldr: Conformalized quantile regression guides hyperparameter search with minimal noise assumptions and improves convergence on empirical benchmarks.

paragraphs: Offline contextual-bandit learning seeks a better decision policy using data already collected by a logging policy. A central challenge is turning that data into a reliable claim about the new policy's performance. This paper develops a learning approach around generalization bounds that are both tighter than competing bounds and tractable to optimize.

The authors use a PAC-Bayesian perspective, representing policies as mixtures of decision rules. This representation supports new bounds and algorithms that optimize those bounds directly. The approach connects the learning objective to a performance guarantee, allowing the method to seek confident improvement over the logging policy using offline observations.

The method uses all available data and does not require tuning extra hyperparameters on held-out sets. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in providing performance guarantees in practical settings. The significance lies in bringing the statistical guarantee into the optimization procedure itself, so that policy learning is guided by an actionable bound rather than by a bound too loose or computationally difficult to use.
icml-2023-pac-bayesian-offline-contextua.tldr: Tractable PAC-Bayesian bounds guide offline contextual-bandit learning toward policies with performance guarantees.

paragraphs: Neural contextual bandits use neural networks in a setting where decisions and learning proceed together. The paper broadens the activation functions considered in this problem: instead of concentrating on ReLU networks, it studies a general collection of smooth activations. This shift requires understanding how the resulting networks relate to their kernel counterparts.

The authors derive finite-size error bounds between an overparameterized neural network and its corresponding neural tangent kernel. These non-asymptotic bounds quantify the approximation rather than relying only on a limiting relationship. That analysis supports a proposed bandit algorithm with a provable sublinear regret bound, so cumulative regret grows slower than the decision horizon.

Empirical studies also demonstrate efficiency in the finite regime, connecting the theoretical development to practically sized settings. The authors suggest that their approximation bounds may have broader value for relating activation smoothness in neural bandits to kernel smoothness in kernel bandits. This potential use is an additional implication of the analysis, alongside the algorithm and its demonstrated performance.
icml-2023-provably-and-practically-effic.tldr: Finite-size neural-kernel error bounds support a smooth-activation contextual-bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and empirical efficiency.

paragraphs: Large diffusion models can be used for malicious image editing. This paper explores a preventive intervention applied to the image itself: adding changes that people cannot perceive but that interfere with a targeted model's editing process. The intended outcome is to make protected images resistant to manipulation by those models.

The protection uses adversarial perturbations designed to disrupt the targeted diffusion models and cause them to generate unrealistic outputs. The authors present two ways to construct these perturbations and demonstrate their efficacy. This turns a model's sensitivity to carefully chosen input changes into a mechanism for obstructing unwanted editing of an image.

The paper also argues that technical perturbations alone are insufficient to make the approach fully effective and practical. It identifies a necessary policy component involving organizations that develop diffusion models, which would implement and support image immunization. The proposed protection therefore combines an image-level technical intervention with developer participation, making institutional support part of the approach rather than placing the entire implementation burden on individual users.
icml-2023-raising-the-cost-of-malicious-.tldr: Imperceptible image perturbations disrupt targeted diffusion-model edits, with developer support identified as necessary for practical effectiveness.

paragraphs: Machine-learned predictions can speed up discrete optimization by supplying useful starting points. Existing runtime guarantees often measure the distance from a prediction to an optimal solution. When a problem has many optima, however, distance to one selected optimum can be misleading: a prediction may be near another equally valid solution.

The paper addresses this issue for L-convex and L-natural-convex function minimization, a setting that includes the dual of bipartite matching. Its framework bounds runtime using distance to the entire set of optimal solutions. This makes the guarantee reflect proximity to any optimum, avoiding arbitrarily large distances caused by choosing an unrepresentative optimal target.

Learning such predictions is the main technical challenge because the desired target is a solution set. The authors provide a method based on online gradient descent and establish polynomial-time learnability of predictions that provably help warm-start optimization despite multiple optima. The contribution aligns the learning goal with what the downstream solver actually needs: a starting point close to some optimal solution.
icml-2023-rethinking-warm-starts-with-pr.tldr: Learning predictions close to optimal-solution sets yields meaningful warm-start guarantees even when discrete optimization problems have many optima.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many observations suffice to recover an unknown high-dimensional simplex when the observations are noisy. Samples are assumed to be independent draws from the uniform distribution over the simplex, corrupted by additive multivariate Gaussian noise. The noise can have arbitrary magnitude, with its effect reflected in the sample requirement.

The authors prove that an algorithm exists which recovers a simplex within any specified positive L2 error tolerance with high probability. Their sufficient sample bound combines dimension and inverse-accuracy factors with an exponential dependence involving dimension divided by squared signal-to-noise ratio. This is a sufficiency result, not a claim that the displayed sample count is necessary.

When signal-to-noise ratio is at least on the order of the square root of dimension, the resulting sample complexity matches the noiseless order. The proofs combine sample compression, high-dimensional geometry, and Fourier analysis. They also introduce a Fourier-based recovery technique for a broader class of distributions under additive Gaussian noise, which may be useful in related recovery problems.
icml-2023-sample-complexity-bounds-for-l.tldr: The paper bounds sufficient samples for recovering a simplex under Gaussian noise and identifies a signal regime matching noiseless sample complexity.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for automatically discovering the structure of Gaussian-process time-series models. It places a Bayesian nonparametric prior over a symbolic model space, so inference concerns which model structures explain the data. The aim is to find accurate models of complex time series through an effective search over that space.

The algorithm combines sequential Monte Carlo with involutive Markov chain Monte Carlo. It supports online learning by incorporating observations as they arrive. It also works offline, progressively using nested subsets of historical observations to anneal the posterior. These two modes let the same structure-learning approach operate with incoming data or a fixed historical collection.

On real-world time series, the method can achieve runtime improvements of 10 to 100 times over previous MCMC and greedy-search methods for the same model family. An evaluation on 1,428 econometric datasets finds sensible discovered models and more accurate point and interval forecasts across multiple horizons than the statistical and neural baselines compared. The findings connect faster structure inference with improved forecasting in this challenging evaluation.
icml-2023-sequential-monte-carlo-learnin.tldr: Combining sequential Monte Carlo and involutive MCMC accelerates Gaussian-process structure discovery and improves forecasts on an econometric benchmark.

paragraphs: Training very large models usually calls for expensive, specialized computing clusters. This paper studies alternatives such as cheaper preemptible instances and resources spread across regions. An analysis of existing model-parallel algorithms identifies configurations in which larger models become less communication-intensive, suggesting that weak network connections need not rule out large-model training.

The proposed SWARM Parallelism algorithm targets devices with uneven capabilities, unreliable availability, and poor connectivity. It creates temporary randomized pipelines between computing nodes and rebalances those pipelines when failures occur. This organization makes adaptation to the available resources part of the training algorithm.

The authors empirically validate their analysis and compare SWARM with existing large-scale training approaches. Combining the approach with compression, they train a Transformer language model with one billion shared parameters, approximately thirteen billion before sharing, on preemptible T4 GPUs with network capacity below 200 Mb/s. The demonstration supports the feasibility of this particular resource-constrained setup; the reduced communication intensity arises in the configurations identified by the analysis.
icml-2023-swarm-parallelism-training-lar.tldr: SWARM uses randomized, rebalanced model-parallel pipelines to train large models on poorly connected and unreliable devices.

paragraphs: Differentially private neural-network training has improved through techniques involving large batches, aggregated data augmentations, and many training steps. These approaches can be computationally expensive, making hyperparameter search difficult. The paper therefore treats private training as a three-way trade-off among privacy, accuracy, and compute, and seeks a cheaper way to explore it.

The authors separate privacy accounting from the experimental behavior of noisy training. Using Rényi differential privacy, they show that the privacy budget depends only on total injected noise when the accounting is not overcharged. This qualified relationship motivates their total amount of noise, or TAN, perspective and scaling laws for choosing DP-SGD hyperparameters.

The proposed method reduces the computational budget for hyperparameter optimization by more than a factor of one hundred. Applications cover CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, with a reported nine-point gain in ImageNet top-1 accuracy over the state of the art at a privacy budget of epsilon eight. These results show how cheaper tuning can improve the practical privacy-accuracy-compute trade-off in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-tan-without-a-burn-scaling-law.tldr: TAN-based scaling laws cut DP-SGD tuning compute by over 100 times and yield a reported nine-point ImageNet accuracy gain at epsilon eight.
